Limits and Derivatives

A derivative is a rate with units. Read it correctly and a 1% index move explains a 7.6% account move.

Volume I · Calculus for FinanceBuilds on LM1Leads to LM3 · LM4 · LM5 · LM7 · LM8 · LM9 · LM12 · LM15 · LM18 · LM20 · LM23 · LM40Time ≈ 2.5 h + labPDF A4 print edition
Learning Outcomes
MasteryAfter this module you should be able to:
1evaluate limits, including one-sided limits and limits at infinity, and identify where a function is discontinuous or not differentiable
2define the derivative as the limit of a difference quotient, and interpret it as a slope, a marginal rate and a sensitivity with units
3derive the power, exponential, logarithmic, product, quotient and chain rules, and apply them to financial functions
4calculate the delta of a futures position, the modified duration of a bond and the rate sensitivity of a present value
5calculate elasticities, and show that the elasticity of a futures account's equity with respect to the futures price equals its leverage, exposure ÷ equity
6estimate changes with differentials, bound the error of a linear approximation, and explain when it fails
7compute derivatives numerically with forward and central differences, and choose a step size that balances truncation and rounding error
8implement and verify derivatives in Python with finite differences and symbolic differentiation
Learning Module Overview
  • A limit describes where a function is heading, not where it is. Two limits carry the whole module, (ex−1)/x→1 and ln(1+x)/x→1 as x→0, and both follow from one inequality and the squeeze theorem.
  • The derivative h′(x0​)=limΔx→0​[h(x0​+Δx)−h(x0​)]/Δx is a rate with units: NT$200 per index point for one TX contract, −0.0898 per 100 face per basis point for a 10-year 2% bond at par.
  • Six rules — power, exponential, logarithm, product, quotient and chain — differentiate every function built from powers, exponentials and logarithms. Each is proved here from the definition.
  • Modified duration is the derivative −P′(y)/P, and Macaulay duration falls out of it. For the 10-year 2% par bond Dmod​=8.9826, which equals its 10-year annuity factor at 2%.
  • Elasticity dlnh/dlnx is a unit-free derivative. A futures account's equity elasticity equals its leverage f = exposure ÷ equity: on 11 June 2025 one TX contract on NT$600,000 had f=7.37 and returned 7.60% on a 1.025% TAIEX day.
  • The leverage of a fixed position is not constant: its own elasticity is 1−f. In April 2025 an account starting at f=4.73 reached f=44.3 in three sessions, while the linear approximation predicted 8.14.
  • Forward differences have truncation error O(Δx), central differences O(Δx2), and rounding adds an error of order εm​/Δx. In double precision the best steps for the bond are near 10−8 and 10−6; a central 1 bp bump gets duration right to within 0.000002.

1Introduction

A derivative answers one question: when an input moves a little, how much does an output move, per unit of input? Traders answer it daily without naming it. One TX contract gains NT$200 per index point; a bond with modified duration 9 loses about 9% per percentage point of yield, to first order.

This module builds the mathematics behind such numbers — limits, derivatives and elasticities — and shows where the linear picture breaks.

Motivating CaseA 1% day that becomes a 7.6% day

On 11 June 2025 TAIEX closed at 22,470.10, up 1.025%. The June TAIEX futures contract (TX) settled at 22,344, up 228 points. TX is marked to market at NT$200 per index point, so each long contract was credited NT$45,600 that evening. It was an ordinary session: 56 of the 145 sessions from 2 April to 31 October 2025 moved more.

Two traders were each long one contract at the previous day's settlement. Trader A had NT$600,000 of account equity and earned +7.60% on the day. Trader B had NT$900,000 and earned +5.07%. Both accounts exceeded an initial margin of NT$350,000 per contract. That margin is an illustrative assumption: TAIFEX resets margins often, and Section 6 quotes a dated official figure.

Two months earlier the same position had been a disaster. On 7 April 2025, the largest daily fall of the sample, TX settled at its −10% daily limit. Trader A lost 71% of equity in one session and Trader B lost 47%.

Why is the multiple 7.4 for one trader and 4.9 for the other? Why does it not stay fixed? And why did a 19% fall in the futures price over three sessions lift B's leverage from 4.7 to 44?

Each answer is one derivative. Section 6 resolves the case, and Section 7 explains why the linear answer failed in April.

Sections 2–4 build the tools: limits, continuity, the derivative and its rules. Section 5 reads derivatives as sensitivities: futures delta, duration, rate risk. Section 6 introduces elasticity, which resolves the case.

Section 7 turns derivatives into approximations and shows how they fail. Section 8 computes derivatives numerically, where rounding makes "a smaller step is better" false, and Section 9 does it in Python.

NoteNotation in this module

f is exposure ÷ equity, so f>1 is leverage. Chosen to maximize growth g(f), it is the Kelly fraction f∗ of LM4; L is a leveraged fund's daily multiple (LM3). Generic functions are h and u of a variable x, as in h(u(x)); x0​ is a point, Δx a step and ℓ a limit.

Local symbols: N contracts with multiplier m (NT$ per index point), futures price F, index S and equity E, so f=NmF/E; Fz​ is the futures price at which equity is zero. In F=Se(rf​−q)τ, rf​ is the continuously compounded financing rate, q the continuous dividend yield and τ the time to expiry in years; T is a bond's or payment's maturity in years. ηh,x​ is an elasticity, Q+​, Q−​, Qc​ are difference quotients and εm​ is machine epsilon. Counts: n periods or payments, j an integer power.

2Limits and Continuity

evaluate limits, including one-sided limits and limits at infinity, and identify where a function is discontinuous or not differentiable

Where a function is heading

The slope of a chord of ex from 0 to x is (ex−1)/x. At x=0 the expression is 0/0 and means nothing. For x=0.01 it is 1.005017, and for x=−0.01 it is 0.995017: the values head toward 1 from both sides. A limit makes "heads toward" precise, and it does not care what happens at the point.

DefinitionLimit

limx→x0​​h(x)=ℓ means that h(x) is as close to ℓ as we like whenever x is close enough to x0​, with x=x0​. Precisely: for every ε>0 there is a δ>0 such that 0<∣x−x0​∣<δ implies ∣h(x)−ℓ∣<ε. The one-sided limits limx→x0−​​ and limx→x0+​​ let x approach from one side only; the limit exists exactly when both exist and agree. limx→∞​h(x)=ℓ means that for every ε>0 there is a number xε​ such that x>xε​ implies ∣h(x)−ℓ∣<ε.

Limits combine as expected: if limh=ℓ1​ and limu=ℓ2​, then lim(h±u)=ℓ1​±ℓ2​, limhu=ℓ1​ℓ2​, and limh/u=ℓ1​/ℓ2​ when ℓ2​=0. These limit laws are stated without proof (Stewart, chapter 2). One more tool does the heavy lifting below.

TheoremSqueeze theorem

If h1​(x)≤h(x)≤h2​(x) for all x=x0​ near x0​, and limx→x0​​h1​(x)=limx→x0​​h2​(x)=ℓ, then limx→x0​​h(x)=ℓ.

Deep DiveThe ε–δ definition at workoptional · click to expand

A limit from the definition. To show limx→2​(3x−1)=5, let ε>0 and choose δ=ε/3. Then 0<∣x−2∣<δ gives ∣(3x−1)−5∣=3∣x−2∣<3δ=ε. The proof is a recipe: given a tolerance ε on the output, produce a tolerance δ on the input.

Proof of the squeeze theorem. Let ε>0. Choose δ so small that 0<∣x−x0​∣<δ implies h1​(x)>ℓ−ε and h2​(x)<ℓ+ε; both are possible because h1​ and h2​ tend to ℓ. On that set ℓ−ε<h1​(x)≤h(x)≤h2​(x)<ℓ+ε, so ∣h(x)−ℓ∣<ε. ■

Continuity

DefinitionContinuity

h is continuous at x0​ if h(x0​) is defined, limx→x0​​h(x) exists, and the two are equal. h is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at each of its points.

Polynomials, ex and lnx (for x>0) are continuous. So are sums, products, quotients and compositions of continuous functions, wherever they are defined. Continuity also lets a limit pass inside a function: if limx→x0​​u(x)=ℓ and h is continuous at ℓ, then limx→x0​​h(u(x))=h(ℓ). All three facts are stated without proof (Stewart, chapter 2).

A function can fail to be continuous in three ways, and each has a financial example.

  • Removable discontinuity. (ex−1)/x is undefined at 0, but its limit exists (it is 1, as shown below). Defining the value at 0 as 1 repairs it.
  • Jump. A digital option pays 1 if the index ends above the strike K and 0 otherwise. Its payoff jumps at K, where the left and right limits are 0 and 1.
  • Infinite discontinuity. The leverage f=NmF/E of a futures account grows without bound as equity approaches zero. For Trader A on 11 June, equity is zero at F=22,116−600,000/200=19,116, and f→+∞ as F falls toward that level.

Continuity is weaker than smoothness. The call payoff max(S−K,0) is continuous at the strike but has a corner there; Section 3 shows that it has no derivative at K.

Two limits that carry the module

By (1.6) of LM1, ex=limn→∞​(1+x/n)n for every real x. Everything we need about the slope of ex then follows from Bernoulli's inequality: for every integer n≥1 and every x≥−1,

(1+x)n≥1+nx.
The proof is by induction. It holds with equality for n=1. If it holds for n, then, because 1+x≥0, (1+x)n+1≥(1+nx)(1+x)=1+(n+1)x+nx2≥1+(n+1)x.

Replace x by x/n with n≥∣x∣: (1+x/n)n≥1+x. Letting n→∞ preserves the inequality, so ex≥1+x for every real x. Applied to −x it gives e−x≥1−x, which is positive when x<1. Since exe−x=1 by the laws of exponents (LM1),

1+x≤ex≤1−x1​(x<1).(2.1)

Subtract 1 and divide by x. For 0<x<1 this gives 1≤(ex−1)/x≤1/(1−x). For x<0 the division flips both inequalities: 1/(1−x)≤(ex−1)/x≤1. In both cases the bounds tend to 1 (Exhibit 2 shows them closing in), so the squeeze theorem yields

x→0lim​xex−1​=1.(2.2)

A second limit follows by substitution. Let z=ln(1+x), so that x=ez−1. As x→0, z→0 because ln is continuous at 1, and z=0 whenever x=0. Then ln(1+x)/x=z/(ez−1)=1/[(ez−1)/z], and the quotient law with (2.2) gives

x→0lim​xln(1+x)​=1.(2.3)

In financial language, (2.2) says that a continuously compounded rate x produces a simple return ex−1 whose ratio to x tends to 1. Equation (2.3) says the same of a log return and a simple return. Both are "≈" statements about small moves; LM3 measures their error.

Limits at infinity

Limits at infinity describe long horizons, such as the value of an income stream that never stops.

Example 1From annuity to perpetuity

An annuity pays 1 at the end of each of n years. At the periodic rate i=2% its present value is the annuity factor an,i​=(1−(1+i)−n)/i, which LM6 derives. Compute an,i​ for n=10, 30, 100 and 1,000, and find its limit as n→∞.

Solution

The values are 8.9826, 22.3965, 43.0984 and 50.0000. Because 0<1/1.02<1, the term 1.02−n tends to 0, and the limit laws give limn→∞​an,i​=1/0.02=50: the value of a perpetuity.

The gap 50−an,i​=50×1.02−n shrinks by the same factor 1/1.02 every year, so convergence is steady but slow. After 100 years, 50−43.0984=6.9016, or 13.80% of the perpetuity's value, is still missing. The 10-year factor, 8.9826, will reappear in Section 5 as the duration of a 10-year bond.

PitfallMarket data have no limits

Prices move in ticks (one TX tick is one index point, NT$200), print at discrete times, and gap. On 7 April 2025 TX settled at its −10% daily limit, 2,129 points below a settlement struck five calendar days earlier. Limits and derivatives belong to a model — a pricing formula, a fitted curve, an account-value function — not to a raw price series. "The derivative of the price path" is a modelling choice and should be stated as one.

導讀極限：看「趨近」，不看「等於」

極限描述的是函數「往哪裡去」，不在乎那一點本身有沒有定義。(ex−1)/x 在 x=0 是 0/0，但從兩邊都被夾到 1（夾擠定理 squeeze theorem），這就是「連續複利 x 很小時，簡單報酬 ex−1≈x」的嚴格版本。不連續有三種：可移除（(ex−1)/x 在 0）、跳躍（二元選擇權在履約價）、無窮（權益趨近 0 時的槓桿）；買權在履約價連續但不可微。記住：市場資料是一格一格跳的，極限與導數是「模型」的性質，不是報價本身的性質。

Knowledge Check 1

Use (2.2) to evaluate limΔt→0​(e0.05Δt−1)/Δt. What does the answer say about a 5% continuously compounded rate over a short period of Δt years?

Answer

Put z=0.05Δt: the expression equals 0.05(ez−1)/z, which tends to 0.05⋅1=0.05. Over a short period of Δt years the simple return e0.05Δt−1 is 0.05Δt up to an error of order Δt2, between 0 and z2/(1−z) by (2.1). The instantaneous growth rate of the investment is 5% a year.

3The Derivative

define the derivative as the limit of a difference quotient, and interpret it as a slope, a marginal rate and a sensitivity with units

From average to instantaneous rate

The average rate of change of h between x0​ and x0​+Δx is the difference quotient [h(x0​+Δx)−h(x0​)]/Δx: the slope of the secant through the two points. As Δx shrinks, the secant pivots about (x0​,h(x0​)). If it settles on a limiting line, that line is the tangent and its slope is the derivative.

DefinitionDerivative

h is differentiable at x0​ if the finite limit

h′(x0​)=Δx→0lim​Δxh(x0​+Δx)−h(x0​)​(2.4)
exists. h′(x0​) is the derivative of h at x0​, also written dxdh​​x=x0​​. If h is differentiable at every point of an interval, x↦h′(x) is a new function; differentiating it again gives the second derivative h′′.

A derivative carries units: output units per input unit. That is why one number answers three questions.

  • Slope (geometry): the steepness of the tangent line.
  • Marginal rate (economics): the extra output from one more unit of input, such as the extra interest from lengthening a loan.
  • Sensitivity (risk): the change in a value per unit change in a risk factor. A TX contract has a sensitivity of NT$200 per index point.

Two derivatives from the definition show the mechanics. For h(x)=x2, [(x+Δx)2−x2]/Δx=2x+Δx→2x. For h(x)=1/x with x=0, [1/(x+Δx)−1/x]/Δx=−1/[x(x+Δx)]→−1/x2.

Example 2A derivative from the definition: the one-year zero

A one-year zero-coupon bond pays 100 at maturity, so its price at annual yield y is P(y)=100/(1+y). Find P′(y) from (2.4) and evaluate it at y=2%. How much does the price fall per basis point for NT$100 million of face value?

Solution

The difference quotient is

Δy1​[1+y+Δy100​−1+y100​]=Δy(1+y)(1+y+Δy)100[(1+y)−(1+y+Δy)]​=(1+y)(1+y+Δy)−100​.
As Δy→0 it tends to P′(y)=−100/(1+y)2. At y=2%, P′(0.02)=−96.1169 per 100 face per unit of yield.

A basis point is 0.0001 units of yield, so the price falls by 0.009612 per 100 face per bp. For NT$100 million of face, that is NT$9,612 per bp. This number — the price fall for a one-basis-point rise in yield — is called the DV01.

The figure below lets you watch the secant become the tangent. Its opening view uses h(x)=ex at x0​=0 with a forward step Δx=0.5: the secant slope is 1.29744 while the tangent slope is 1. Shrink Δx and the error falls in proportion to Δx; switch to central differences and it falls in proportion to Δx2.

Real pricing functions behave the same way. Exhibit 3 applies (2.4) to the price of a 10-year bond with a 2% annual coupon, valued at a 2% yield, where it trades at par. Section 5 derives the exact derivative, P′(2%)=−898.2585.

Differentiable implies continuous

If h is differentiable at x0​, then h(x0​+Δx)−h(x0​)=Δx⋅Δxh(x0​+Δx)−h(x0​)​→0⋅h′(x0​)=0, so h is continuous at x0​. The converse fails.

The one-sided derivatives h±′​(x0​)=limΔx→0±​[h(x0​+Δx)−h(x0​)]/Δx can exist and differ. For the call payoff max(S−K,0) the right derivative at K is 1 and the left derivative is 0. The payoff therefore has no derivative at K. The digital payoff is not even continuous at K, so it cannot be differentiable there.

The mean value theorem

TheoremMean value theorem

If h is continuous on [x1​,x2​] and differentiable on (x1​,x2​), there is a point ξ∈(x1​,x2​) with

h′(ξ)=x2​−x1​h(x2​)−h(x1​)​.

Somewhere, the instantaneous rate equals the average rate. When the bond's yield rises from 2% to 3%, its price falls from 100 to 91.469797, an average slope of −853.0203 per unit of yield. The theorem guarantees a yield between 2% and 3% at which P′ takes exactly that value.

Two consequences are used repeatedly. If h′>0 on an interval, h is increasing there. If ∣h′∣≤M on [x1​,x2​], then ∣h(x2​)−h(x1​)∣≤M∣x2​−x1​∣, which is how Sections 7 and 8 bound errors.

Deep DiveProof of the mean value theoremoptional · click to expand

Rolle's theorem. Suppose also that h(x1​)=h(x2​). A continuous function on a closed interval attains a maximum and a minimum (the extreme value theorem, stated without proof).

If both occur at the endpoints, h is constant and h′=0 everywhere. Otherwise an extremum, say a maximum, occurs at an interior point ξ. There [h(ξ+Δx)−h(ξ)]/Δx≤0 for Δx>0 and ≥0 for Δx<0, so the limit h′(ξ) is both ≤0 and ≥0: h′(ξ)=0.

The general case. Apply Rolle's theorem to H(x)=h(x)−h(x1​)−x2​−x1​h(x2​)−h(x1​)​(x−x1​), which satisfies H(x1​)=H(x2​)=0. Some ξ∈(x1​,x2​) has H′(ξ)=h′(ξ)−x2​−x1​h(x2​)−h(x1​)​=0. ■

PitfallPer unit, per percent, per basis point

P′(2%)=−898.2585 is a price change per unit of yield, that is, per 100 percentage points. Per percentage point it is −8.98; per basis point it is −0.0898. Futures delta has the same trap: NT$200 per index point for one TX contract, but NT$44,688 per 1% move at F=22,344. Most sensitivity errors in practice are unit errors, so write the units next to every derivative.

Knowledge Check 2

Use the definition (2.4) to find the derivative of h(x)=x3 at x=2.

Answer

(2+Δx)3−8=12Δx+6Δx2+Δx3, so the difference quotient is 12+6Δx+Δx2, which tends to 12. Hence h′(2)=12, in agreement with the power rule of Section 4.

4Differentiation Rules

derive the power, exponential, logarithmic, product, quotient and chain rules, and apply them to financial functions

Six rules, each proved once from (2.4), differentiate every function built from powers, exponentials and logarithms by sums, products, quotients and compositions.

Linearity and integer powers

From the limit laws, (κh)′=κh′ for any constant κ, and (h+u)′=h′+u′: differentiation is linear. For a positive integer j, the binomial theorem gives (x+Δx)j=xj+jxj−1Δx+Δx2×(a polynomial in x and Δx). Dividing by Δx and letting Δx→0 leaves dxd​xj=jxj−1.

The exponential and the logarithm

PropositionDerivatives of eκx and lnx

For any constant κ,

dxd​eκx=κeκxfor all x,dxd​lnx=x1​for x>0.

Proof. For κ=0, the law of exponents gives [eκ(x+Δx)−eκx]/Δx=κeκx(eκΔx−1)/(κΔx), which tends to κeκx by (2.2) with κΔx in place of x. For κ=0 both sides are 0.

For the logarithm, ln(x+Δx)−lnx=ln(1+Δx/x). With z=Δx/x,

Δxln(x+Δx)−lnx​=x1​⋅zln(1+z)​⟶x1​⋅1
by (2.3), since z→0 as Δx→0. ■

With κ=1, the exponential is its own rate of change. Wealth W(t)=W0​egt grows at W′(t)=gW(t): a constant proportional rate g, the log growth rate of LM1. Its logarithm, lnW(t)=lnW0​+gt, is a straight line with slope g.

Products and quotients

PropositionProduct and quotient rules

If u and h are differentiable at x, then (uh)′=u′h+uh′, and, where h(x)=0, (u/h)′=(u′h−uh′)/h2.

Proof. Add and subtract u(x)h(x+Δx):

Δxu(x+Δx)h(x+Δx)−u(x)h(x)​=Δxu(x+Δx)−u(x)​h(x+Δx)+u(x)Δxh(x+Δx)−h(x)​.
Because h is differentiable, it is continuous, so h(x+Δx)→h(x) and the right side tends to u′h+uh′. For the quotient, first
Δx1​[h(x+Δx)1​−h(x)1​]=−Δxh(x+Δx)−h(x)​⋅h(x+Δx)h(x)1​⟶−h2h′​,
and then the product rule applied to u⋅(1/h) gives u′/h−uh′/h2=(u′h−uh′)/h2. ■

The chain rule

Most pricing functions are nested: a bond price depends on discount factors, which depend on the yield. The chain rule differentiates compositions.

TheoremChain rule

If u is differentiable at x and h is differentiable at u(x), then h(u(x)) is differentiable at x and

dxd​h(u(x))=h′(u(x))u′(x),ordxdh​=dudh​⋅dxdu​.(2.5)

The intuitive argument writes Δh/Δx=(Δh/Δu)(Δu/Δx) and lets Δx→0. It is correct whenever Δu=0 for small Δx, which can fail if u oscillates. The Deep Dive gives a proof without that gap.

Deep DiveA proof of the chain rule without dividing by zerooptional · click to expand

Lemma (Carathéodory). h is differentiable at x0​ if and only if h(x)−h(x0​)=hˉ(x)(x−x0​) near x0​ for some function hˉ continuous at x0​. Then hˉ(x0​)=h′(x0​). If h is differentiable, set hˉ(x)=[h(x)−h(x0​)]/(x−x0​) for x=x0​ and hˉ(x0​)=h′(x0​); continuity of hˉ at x0​ is the definition (2.4). Conversely, dividing by x−x0​ and letting x→x0​ gives h′(x0​)=hˉ(x0​).

Proof of (2.5). Let z0​=u(x0​). Write u(x)−u(x0​)=uˉ(x)(x−x0​) and h(z)−h(z0​)=hˉ(z)(z−z0​), with uˉ continuous at x0​ and hˉ continuous at z0​. Then

h(u(x))−h(u(x0​))=hˉ(u(x))(u(x)−u(x0​))=hˉ(u(x))uˉ(x)(x−x0​).
The factor hˉ(u(x))uˉ(x) is continuous at x0​, because u is continuous at x0​, and its value there is hˉ(z0​)uˉ(x0​)=h′(u(x0​))u′(x0​). By the lemma, h(u(x)) is differentiable at x0​ with that derivative. ■

The chain rule completes the toolkit.

  • Real powers. For x>0, xα=eαlnx, so dxd​xα=eαlnx⋅α/x=αxα−1 for any real α.
  • Other bases. For a base β>0, βx=exlnβ, so dxd​βx=βxlnβ.
  • Discount factors. dyd​(1+y)−t=−t(1+y)−t−1 and drd​e−rt=−te−rt.
  • Logarithmic derivative. For h>0, dxd​lnh(x)=h′(x)/h(x): the relative rate of change, the basis of elasticities in Section 6.

Exhibit 4 collects the rules with the places they appear in this book.

Example 3Forward rates from a yield curve

A continuously compounded zero-coupon yield curve is y(T)=2.0%−0.8%e−T/3 for maturity T in years (an illustrative curve, not market data). The discount factor is P(T)=e−y(T)T. The instantaneous forward rate r(T):=−dTd​lnP(T) is the marginal rate earned by extending a deposit's maturity beyond T. Find r(T) and evaluate it at T=1, 5 and 10.

Solution

Since lnP(T)=−y(T)T, the product rule gives r(T)=y(T)+Ty′(T). The derivative of e−T/3 is −31​e−T/3, so y′(T)=30.8%​e−T/3.

T y(T) y′(T) per year r(T)=y+Ty′
1 1.42677% 0.191075% 1.61785%
5 1.84890% 0.050367% 2.10073%
10 1.97146% 0.009513% 2.06659%

The forward rate exceeds the yield wherever the curve slopes up. The yield is an average rate over [0,T]; the forward rate is the marginal rate at T. Whenever a total equals T times an average, marginal=average+T×slope of the average.

Example 4How leverage changes with the futures price

An account holds N contracts with multiplier m, opened at F0​ with equity E0​. Its equity is E(F)=E0​+Nm(F−F0​) and its leverage, exposure ÷ equity, is f(F)=NmF/E(F). Use the quotient rule to find f′(F). Evaluate it for Trader A on 10 June 2025 (N=1, m=200, F0​=22,116, E0​= NT$600,000).

Solution

The quotient rule gives

f′(F)=E2NmE−NmF⋅Nm​=E2Nm(E−NmF)​=Ff​(1−f).
For Trader A, f=4,423,200/600,000=7.3720, so f′(F0​)=−7.3720×6.3720/22,116=−0.0021240 per index point. A 100-point rise should cut leverage by about 0.2124. Exact repricing gives f(22,216)=4,443,200/620,000=7.1665, a fall of 0.2055.

For f>1 the derivative is negative: a fixed long position deleverages as the market rises and leverages up as it falls. Section 6 turns this into a one-line elasticity, and Section 7 shows how it misbehaves in a crash.

導讀連鎖律：敏感度相乘

很多定價函數是「一層套一層」：債券價格 → 折現因子 → 殖利率；台幣價值 → 美元價值 × 匯率。連鎖律說：外層對內層的敏感度，乘上內層對變數的敏感度，就是整體的敏感度。乘法法則與除法法則看起來是代數，其實是「邊際 = 平均 + 期限 × 平均的斜率」（遠期利率）和「槓桿隨價格變動」這類金融結論的來源。後面的 Greeks、存續期間與 LM37 的 Itô 引理，全部建立在連鎖律之上。

Knowledge Check 3

Differentiate ln(1+fR) with respect to f, treating the return R as a constant. What is the derivative at f=0?

Answer

By the chain rule, dfd​ln(1+fR)=R/(1+fR), which equals R at f=0. Averaged over the possible returns, this derivative is g′(f), the slope of the growth curve g(f) of LM4; its zero is the Kelly fraction f∗.

5Derivatives as Sensitivities

calculate the delta of a futures position, the modified duration of a bond and the rate sensitivity of a present value

In risk management a derivative is a sensitivity: the change in a value per unit change in one risk factor, other factors held fixed. This section computes three that desks quote daily: futures delta, bond duration and the rate sensitivity of a present value.

Delta of a futures position

An account holding N contracts opened at F0​ with equity E0​ has equity E(F)=E0​+Nm(F−F0​) after marking to market. Its derivative is the position's delta:

E′(F)=NmNT$ per index point.
The sensitivity is constant because E is linear in F. By linearity of the derivative, the delta of several positions is the sum of their deltas. Exhibit 5 lists the three TAIEX futures contracts.

Delta per index point converts to delta per 1% move by multiplying by F/100. At F=22,344 a 1% move is 223.44 points, worth NT$44,688 to one TX contract. The quantity NmF is the position's notional, or exposure, and "NT$ per 1%" is notional ÷ 100.

Example 5Delta of a mixed position

A trader is long 2 TX, short 3 MTX and long 4 TMF, all in the same expiry month. Compute the position's delta, its profit on a 150-point rise, its delta per 1% move at F=22,344, and the TMF trade that makes it delta-neutral.

Solution

Delta is 2×200−3×50+4×10=290 NT$ per point, the same exposure as 1.45 TX contracts. A 150-point rise earns 150×290= NT$43,500. Per 1% move, delta is 290×223.44= NT$64,798. Selling 29 TMF (29×10=290) brings delta to zero. All of this is exact, because each contract's value is linear in F.

Duration: the derivative of a bond price

A bond with annual cash flows CFt​ at t=1,…,n is priced at yield y as P(y)=∑t​CFt​(1+y)−t. By linearity and the discount-factor rule,

P′(y)=−t=1∑n​tCFt​(1+y)−t−1=−1+y1​t=1∑n​tPVt​,PVt​:=CFt​(1+y)−t.
Dividing by −P defines the modified duration and reveals the Macaulay duration inside it:
Dmod​:=−P(y)P′(y)​=1+yDMac​​,DMac​:=t=1∑n​twt​,wt​:=PPVt​​.(2.6)
Macaulay duration is the present-value-weighted average time of the cash flows. It is not an extra definition: it is what the derivative of the price function produces.

As a sensitivity, (2.6) says ΔP/P≈−Dmod​Δy, with an error of order Δy2 (Section 7). The price fall for a one-basis-point rise in yield, −P′(y)×0.0001, is the bond's DV01. LM3 adds the second-order term, convexity.

Example 6Duration of the 10-year bond as a derivative

The 10-year bond of Exhibit 3 pays a 2% annual coupon and yields 2%. Compute P′(2%), Dmod​, DMac​ and the DV01 for NT$100 million of face. Then compare the first-order estimate of the price change with exact repricing for yield changes of ±25 bp.

Solution

With coupons of 2 and principal 100, P(0.02)=100 and P′(0.02)=−∑t=110​2t/1.02t+1−1000/1.0211=−898.2585. So Dmod​=8.982585 and DMac​=1.02×8.982585=9.1622 years; the final payment alone carries weight w10​=0.8368. The DV01 is 0.08983 per 100 face, or NT$89,826 per NT$100 million.

For Δy=+25 bp the first-order estimate is −8.982585×0.0025=−2.2456%; exact repricing gives −2.2166%. For −25 bp the estimate is +2.2456% and the exact change +2.2753%. The exact changes are asymmetric, while the linear estimate is symmetric and too pessimistic on both sides, by about 3 bp of price. That asymmetry is convexity, the subject of LM3.

The duration 8.9826 equals the 10-year annuity factor of Example 1. This is no coincidence: a bond at par has Dmod​=(1−(1+y)−n)/y (Practice Problem 9).

Rate sensitivity of a present value

For a single payment due in T years, the sensitivity depends on the compounding convention. At a continuously compounded rate r, PV=e−rT per unit of payment and dPV/dr=−T⋅PV: the relative sensitivity is exactly T. At an annually compounded rate y, PV=(1+y)−T and dPV/dy=−1+yT​PV. For NT$1,000,000 due in 5 years at 2%, the sensitivities are −452.42 and −443.99 per bp, on present values of 904,837.42 and 905,730.81.

The same reasoning applies to the index futures fair value F=Se(rf​−q)τ, which LM6 derives by no-arbitrage. Holding rf​, q and τ fixed, dF/dS=e(rf​−q)τ, close to 1.

Holding S, rf​ and τ fixed, dF/dq=−τF. For a three-month contract (τ=0.25) at F=22,000, a rise of 0.1 percentage point in the expected dividend yield lowers fair value by 5.50 points. A derivative that holds the other inputs fixed is a partial derivative, treated properly in LM7.

Knowledge Check 4

A trader is long 3 MTX and short 1 TX. What is the position's delta, and what is its profit if the futures price falls 120 points?

Answer

Delta is 3×50−200=−50 NT$ per point: the position is net short. A 120-point fall earns (−50)×(−120)= NT$6,000.

6Elasticity and Leverage

calculate elasticities, and show that the elasticity of a futures account's equity with respect to the futures price equals its leverage, exposure ÷ equity

A unit-free derivative

A delta of NT$200 per point cannot be compared with a duration of 9 years, and neither says what happens to an account in percent. Elasticity removes units by comparing relative changes.

DefinitionElasticity

For a positive function h of a positive variable x, the elasticity of h with respect to x is

ηh,x​:=dx/xdh/h​=h(x)xh′(x)​=dlnxdlnh​.(2.7)
It is the percentage change in h per 1% change in x, to first order.

The last form follows from the chain rule. Put z=lnx, so x=ez and lnh=lnh(ez). Then dzdlnh​=h(ez)h′(ez)ez​=h(x)xh′(x)​.

Because elasticities are derivatives of logarithms, the rules of Section 4 become rules of addition and multiplication. For positive functions u and h:

  • power: if h is proportional to xα, then ηh,x​=α;
  • product and quotient: ηuh​=ηu​+ηh​ and ηu/h​=ηu​−ηh​;
  • chain: the elasticity of h(u(x)) with respect to x is ηh,u​⋅ηu,x​;
  • sum: ηu+h​=u+hu​ηu​+u+hh​ηh​, a value-weighted average.

The first three follow from ln(uh)=lnu+lnh, lnxα=αlnx and (2.5). For the sum, ηu+h​=u+hx(u′+h′)​=u+hu​⋅uxu′​+u+hh​⋅hxh′​.

The sum rule is why portfolio sensitivities aggregate by value weights. A portfolio 60% in an index fund (elasticity 1) and 40% in cash (elasticity 0) has elasticity 0.6. Exhibit 6 gives each rule a financial reading.

The elasticity of a futures account is its leverage

An account holding N contracts has equity E(F)=E0​+Nm(F−F0​), so E′(F)=Nm. By (2.7),

ηE,F​=EF⋅Nm​=ENmF​=f.(2.8)
The elasticity of equity with respect to the futures price is the notional divided by equity: the account's leverage. Because E is linear in F, the one-day relation is exact, not approximate: ΔE/E=NmΔF/E=f⋅ΔF/F.

The index enters through the chain rule. With the cost-of-carry price F=Se(rf​−q)τ and rf​, q, τ fixed, ηF,S​=Se(rf​−q)τ/F=1. Therefore ηE,S​=ηE,F​ηF,S​=f.

ResultEquity elasticity equals leverage

For a futures account, ηE,F​=f=NmF/E exactly, and under cost of carry ηE,S​=f. The same identity holds for any position financed with fixed debt. If a position worth V is funded by equity E and debt V−E, then ηE,V​=V/E=f.

This covers margin purchases. Buy 1,000 shares of 0050 at an illustrative NT$60 with NT$24,000 of your own and NT$36,000 borrowed: f=60,000/24,000=2.50, so a 4% fall removes 10% of equity.

Example 7Resolving the motivating case

Use (2.8) and Exhibit 1 to explain both traders' returns on 11 June and on 7 April 2025. Then explain the ratio of each account's return to TAIEX's.

Solution

On 11 June the notional at the previous settlement was 200×22,116= NT$4,423,200. So f=4,423,200/600,000=7.3720 for A and 4,423,200/900,000=4.9147 for B. The futures return was +1.0309%, so A earned 7.3720×1.0309%=7.600% and B earned 4.9147×1.0309%=5.067%, exactly as observed.

Against TAIEX's +1.0249%, the ratios are 7.600/1.0249=7.415 and 5.067/1.0249=4.944. They differ slightly from f because the futures and the index moved by different percentages. The ratio of their returns, a measured ηF,S​, was 1.0309/1.0249=1.0059. On 7 April it was 1.0307, and the same arithmetic gives 7.0987×(−9.9972%)=−70.967% for A and 4.7324×(−9.9972%)=−47.311% for B.

Over the 145 sessions from 2 April to 31 October 2025, a least-squares line through daily TX and TAIEX returns has slope 1.008 (correlation 0.978). Day by day the ratio scatters: on the 14 days when TAIEX moved between 0.9% and 1.1% in size, it ranged from 0.753 to 1.459.

TAIEX closes on a 13:25–13:30 call auction; the TX settlement comes from the last minute of trading to 13:45. The basis also moves with dividend expectations. On average the measured ηF,S​ is close to 1; on any one day it is noisy.

The answer to "why 5–8%?" is therefore not the contract but the equity behind it: the multiple is notional ÷ equity. With the illustrative initial margin of NT$350,000 as the only equity, f on 11 June would have been 12.64.

The exchange's margins cap leverage. TAIFEX's table effective 12 August 2026 requires an initial margin of NT$701,000 and a maintenance margin of NT$538,000 per TX contract. The MTX and TMF figures, NT$175,250 and NT$35,050 initial, are exactly 1/4 and 1/20 of TX, in proportion to the multipliers.

TAIFEX recalculates margin levels after each regular session and may adjust them when the change reaches a set threshold. That is why this module uses an illustrative 2025 figure rather than a quoted one. Scaled by TAIFEX's ratio 538,000/701,000, the illustrative initial margin of NT$350,000 corresponds to an illustrative maintenance margin of about NT$268,600.

Leverage moves: its elasticity is 1−f

Leverage is a ratio, so its elasticity follows from the quotient rule for elasticities and (2.8):

ηf,F​=ηF,F​−ηE,F​=1−f.(2.9)
This is the elasticity form of Example 4. For f>1 it is negative.

A 1% rise in the futures price cuts Trader A's leverage of 7.3720 by about 6.4%, to a first-order 6.9023. The exact value is 6.9345. On 11 June itself, a 1.0309% rise took A from 7.3720 to 6.9219, against a linear prediction of 6.8877.

Over months the drift is large. Exhibit 7 follows both accounts from the close of 10 June to 31 October 2025, holding one near-month contract and rolling the day before each expiry. TAIEX rose 26.94% and the futures position gained 6,824 points, or NT$1,364,800. A's leverage fell from 7.37 to 2.89 and B's from 4.91 to 2.51.

Despite falling leverage, A's equity rose 227.47% and B's 151.64%. A fixed position's profit is linear in index points. Its return on the initial equity is therefore f0​ times the points gained divided by F0​: 7.3720×6,824/22,116=227.47%. Multiplying f0​ by TAIEX's return would have predicted only 7.3720×26.94%≈198.6%.

The futures also gained 832.79 more points than the index (6,824 against 5,991.21). The rolls added a net 510 points: +565 from the June, July and August rolls into cheaper contracts, −55 from the September and October rolls. The other 322.79 points came from the basis, which moved from a 126.14-point discount on 10 June to a 196.65-point premium on 31 October. LM6 explains this basis.

Pitfall"My leverage is 7" is a statement about today

Leverage, like any elasticity, is local. A fixed number of contracts deleverages in a rally and leverages up in a sell-off, at the rate 1−f of (2.9). A daily-reset fund with multiple L does the opposite: it trades every day to hold f=L, which produces the volatility drag of LM3. Neither is "the" leverage, so a risk limit of "at most f=5" must say how often the position is rebalanced back to 5.

Example 8The measured elasticity of 00631L to 0050

00631L is designed to return twice the daily return of the Taiwan 50 index (L=2), which 0050 tracks. Using daily total returns from 3 November 2014 to 8 October 2026, estimate its elasticity with respect to 0050, and comment.

Solution

To first order in R0050​, R00631L​≈ηR0050​. The slope of a least-squares line through the 2,902 pairs of daily returns therefore estimates an average daily elasticity (LM23 treats regression).

Each fund split after a trading halt: 0050 4-for-1 on 18 June 2025 and 00631L 22-for-1 on 31 March 2026. The previous close is restated per new share, and returns run between common trading dates, so two pairs span the halts (six and five sessions). Unadjusted closes would give a slope of 0.846.

The slope is 1.887 and the correlation 0.974, with or without the two halt pairs. By full calendar year it ranged from 1.717 (2024) to 1.984 (2021).

On 7 April 2025 both funds closed at their daily price limits: 0050 fell 10.000% and 00631L 19.995%. TWSE sets the limit of a leveraged ETF on a domestic index at 10% times its multiple, so 00631L's is 20%. That day's ratio of 2.000 therefore reflects the exchange's limits, not the fund. The next session 0050 fell 3.25% and 00631L 11.20%, a ratio of 3.45.

The designed elasticity is 2; the measured one is lower on average. One likely source is replication basis, which LM3 discusses for the fund's long-run returns: the fund holds mostly TAIEX futures rather than Taiwan 50 instruments. Its market price can also drift from its net asset value. A designed elasticity still has to be measured.

Example 9A TWD investor in a USD asset

A Taiwan investor holds a US equity fund. Over a quarter the fund returns RUSD=+6.00% in USD, while the exchange rate X, TWD per USD, returns RFX=−6.00% (illustrative numbers). Compute the investor's TWD return exactly and to first order, and describe what a currency hedge changes.

Solution

The TWD value is V=VUSD×X, so by the product rule its elasticity with respect to each factor is 1. Log returns add exactly, as in (1.15) of LM1: rTWD=ln1.06+ln0.94=−0.00361, a simple return of 1.06×0.94−1=−0.36%.

The first-order answer, 6%−6%=0, misses the second-order cross term RUSDRFX=−0.36%. Selling the initial USD value forward replaces most of the currency return with the forward premium (LM6). The hedge is not exact: the 6% gain in USD stays exposed to the exchange rate.

導讀彈性 = 槓桿倍數

彈性是「百分比對百分比」的導數，沒有單位，所以能比較台指期、債券與外幣資產。期貨帳戶權益數對期貨價格的彈性，恰好等於名目價值（契約價值）÷ 權益數 =f，同一口台指期，掛在 60 萬權益數上是 7.37 倍，掛在 90 萬上只有 4.91 倍，所以 1% 的行情變成 7.6% 或 5.1%。關鍵是 f 本身也會動：ηf,F​=1−f，固定口數時，漲了自動降槓桿，跌了槓桿暴增。每日重設的槓桿 ETF 反過來每天調整部位維持固定倍數 L，這就是 LM3 波動拖累 (volatility drag) 的來源。

Knowledge Check 5

An account holds one TX contract with f=6. Estimate its leverage after a 1% rise in the futures price, then compute it exactly.

Answer

By (2.9) the elasticity is 1−6=−5, so f falls by about 5%, to 6×0.95=5.70. Exactly, the new notional is 1.01 times the old and equity is 1+6×0.01=1.06 times the old, so f=6×1.01/1.06=5.7170.

7Differentials and Linear Approximation

estimate changes with differentials, bound the error of a linear approximation, and explain when it fails

The differential

A derivative turns into an approximation by running the definition backwards. If Δx is small, h(x0​+Δx)−h(x0​) is close to h′(x0​)Δx.

DefinitionDifferential and linear approximation

If h is differentiable at x0​, the differential dh=h′(x0​)dx is the change along the tangent line for an input change dx. The linear approximation of h at x0​ is T1​(x):=h(x0​)+h′(x0​)(x−x0​), the first-order Taylor polynomial of LM3.

By the definition of the derivative, the error err(x):=h(x)−T1​(x) satisfies err(x)/(x−x0​)→0: it vanishes faster than the step. When h has a bounded second derivative, the mean value theorem makes this quantitative.

ResultSize of the linearization error

If h is twice differentiable between x0​ and x, with ∣h′′∣≤M there, then

​h(x)−T1​(x)​≤M(x−x0​)2.(2.10)
The error of a linear approximation is O((x−x0​)2): halve the step and the bound falls by a factor of 4.

Proof. By the mean value theorem, h(x)−h(x0​)=h′(ξ)(x−x0​) for some ξ between x0​ and x. Hence err(x)=[h′(ξ)−h′(x0​)](x−x0​). Applying the theorem to h′ gives h′(ξ)−h′(x0​)=h′′(ζ)(ξ−x0​), and ∣ξ−x0​∣≤∣x−x0​∣. ■ LM3 sharpens the constant from M to M/2 and gives the error exactly.

Linearizing ex at 0 gives errors ex−(1+x) of 0.021403, 0.005171 and 0.001271 for x=0.2, 0.1 and 0.05. Each halving divides the error by about four (4.14, then 4.07).

When the linear approximation fails

The bound (2.10) names the two enemies: a large step ∣x−x0​∣ and a large curvature M. Four situations defeat a tangent line.

  1. Large moves. The error grows like the square of the move. A tangent fitted at today's yield or price is a local tool.
  2. Singularities. Near a point where h blows up, M is huge and no tangent follows the curve. Leverage near the zero-equity level is the example below.
  3. Kinks and jumps. At a corner, such as a call payoff at the strike, no tangent exists. Across a jump, such as a gap or a limit-locked session, no continuous model applies.
  4. Stationary points. If h′(x0​)=0, the tangent is flat and says nothing about the direction of change. The second derivative decides, which is the business of LM4 (optima) and LM3 (convexity).

April 2025 shows the second case in real data. Trader B held one April contract on NT$900,000 at the close of 2 April, with f=4.732. Equity reaches zero at Fz​=F0​−E0​/(Nm)=21,296−900,000/200=16,796, where f has a vertical asymptote. Exhibit 8 compares B's exact leverage with the linear approximation f(F0​)+f′(F0​)(F−F0​) built on 2 April from Example 4.

For a hypothetical 1% fall from 2 April, the linear estimate (4.9091) misses the exact value (4.9179) by 0.0088. For the 19.31% fall to 9 April it predicts 8.143 when the truth is 44.289. The derivative at 2 April was correct; it simply stopped describing the function. Near Fz​, f behaves like 1/(F−Fz​), whose curvature explodes.

In practice neither account would have stayed untouched. A margin call comes when equity falls below the maintenance margin, illustratively NT$268,600 here. A's equity fell below it after 7 April (NT$174,200). B stayed above it after 8 April (NT$274,600) and fell far below it after 9 April (NT$77,600); either trader then had to deposit more or close the position.

導讀線性近似什麼時候會失效

線性近似（切線）的誤差和「步長平方 × 曲率」同階，所以有四種情況會失效：變動太大、靠近奇異點（曲率爆炸）、尖角或跳空（根本沒有切線）、以及導數剛好為 0 的駐點。2025 年 4 月的台指期就是第二種：B 帳戶 4/2 槓桿 4.73 倍，三個交易日後期貨跌 19.3%，用切線估計只會到 8.1 倍，實際卻是 44.3 倍，因為權益數逼近 0，槓桿在「權益歸零點」16,796 有垂直漸近線。結論：導數是「當下」的敏感度，大行情時要重新計算，不能拿昨天的 delta 或 duration 線性外推。

Knowledge Check 6

Use a differential to estimate the price change, per 100 face, of the 10-year 2% bond when its yield rises from 2.00% to 2.05%.

Answer

dP=P′(0.02)dy=−898.2585×0.0005=−0.4491. Exact repricing gives −0.4480; the difference is the second-order convexity effect of LM3.

8Numerical Differentiation

compute derivatives numerically with forward and central differences, and choose a step size that balances truncation and rounding error

Many pricing functions are code with no usable derivative formula: a callable bond on a tree, a Monte Carlo option value, an interpolated curve. Practitioners then bump and reprice: they evaluate the function at nearby inputs and form a difference quotient. Doing this well requires knowing two errors that pull in opposite directions.

Forward and central differences

For a step Δx>0, the forward, backward and central difference quotients are

Q+​(Δx)=Δxh(x+Δx)−h(x)​,Q−​(Δx)=Δxh(x)−h(x−Δx)​,Qc​(Δx)=2Δxh(x+Δx)−h(x−Δx)​.​(2.11)
The central quotient is the average of the other two.

Truncation error of the forward quotient. By the mean value theorem, Q+​(Δx)=h′(ξ) for some ξ∈(x,x+Δx). Applying the theorem again to h′, Q+​(Δx)−h′(x)=h′(ξ)−h′(x)=h′′(ζ)(ξ−x). If ∣h′′∣≤M2​ near x, then ∣Q+​(Δx)−h′(x)∣≤M2​Δx: the error is O(Δx).

Truncation error of the central quotient. If ∣h′′′∣≤M3​ near x, then ∣Qc​(Δx)−h′(x)∣≤M3​Δx2: the error is O(Δx2). The odd symmetry of the central quotient cancels the first-order error term. The Deep Dive proves it with the mean value theorem alone.

Deep DiveWhy the central difference is second orderoptional · click to expand

Let J(θ)=h(x+θ)−h(x−θ), so J(0)=0 and Qc​(Δx)=J(Δx)/(2Δx). By the mean value theorem, J(Δx)=ΔxJ′(θ) for some θ∈(0,Δx), and J′(θ)=h′(x+θ)+h′(x−θ). Therefore

Qc​(Δx)−h′(x)=21​[(h′(x+θ)−h′(x))−(h′(x)−h′(x−θ))]=2θ​[h′′(ξ1​)−h′′(ξ2​)]
with ξ1​∈(x,x+θ) and ξ2​∈(x−θ,x), using the theorem on h′ twice. Once more, ∣h′′(ξ1​)−h′′(ξ2​)∣≤M3​∣ξ1​−ξ2​∣≤2θM3​, hence ∣Qc​(Δx)−h′(x)∣≤θ2M3​≤M3​Δx2. ■

Taylor's theorem in LM3 sharpens the constants: the forward error is 21​h′′(x)Δx and the central error 61​h′′′(x)Δx2, up to higher-order terms.

The orders are visible in the numbers. For h(x)=ex at 0, the forward error divided by Δx is 0.5171, 0.5084 and 0.5042 for Δx=0.1, 0.05 and 0.025, approaching h′′(0)/2=0.5. The central error divided by Δx2 is 0.16675, 0.16669 and 0.16667, approaching h′′′(0)/6=1/6.

Rounding error and the best step

Double precision stores about 16 significant digits. The gap between 1 and the next representable number is machine epsilon, εm​=2.22×10−16, so each computed h(x±Δx) carries a rounding error of order εm​∣h(x)∣. Subtracting two nearly equal values keeps those errors while the true difference shrinks, and dividing by Δx magnifies them.

The total error of the forward quotient is therefore about

err+​(Δx)≈21​∣h′′∣Δx+Δx2εm​∣h∣​,minimized at Δx+∗​=2εm​∣h∣/∣h′′∣​,
and that of the central quotient about
errc​(Δx)≈61​∣h′′′∣Δx2+Δxεm​∣h∣​,minimized at Δxc∗​=(3εm​∣h∣/∣h′′′∣)1/3.
These are order-of-magnitude models, with the truncation constants taken from LM3. The lessons are robust: the best forward step scales like εm​​=1.5×10−8, the best central step like εm1/3​=6.1×10−6, each times the scale of the problem.

For the bond, ∣P∣=100, P′′(2%)=9,399.5462 and P′′′(2%)=−108,918.1833. The models give Δy+∗​≈3×10−9 and Δyc∗​≈8×10−7. Exhibit 9 scans Δy from 10−16 to 10−1; the smallest errors occur at Δy=10−8.25 (forward, relative error 2.4×10−8) and Δy=10−5.75 (central, relative error 6.1×10−12).

Example 10Duration by bumping the yield

Estimate the modified duration of the 10-year bond by bumping its yield 1 bp, first with a forward and then with a central difference. Compare both with the exact value.

Solution

With Δy=0.0001, the forward estimate is −Q+​(Δy)/P=8.977887, an error of −0.004698. The central estimate is −Qc​(Δy)/P=8.9825868, against the exact 8.9825850: an error of +1.8×10−6. The central bump is about 2,600 times more accurate at the cost of one extra pricing.

This is why effective duration, [P(y−Δy)−P(y+Δy)]/[2ΔyP(y)] for a parallel shift Δy of the yield curve, is a central difference. A 1 bp step is far above the rounding floor, so it is safe for any well-behaved pricer.

PitfallSmaller is not better, and kinks fool every formula

Shrinking the step below the optimum makes the estimate worse, as Exhibit 10 shows at Δy=10−12. At a kink no step helps. For the call payoff max(x−1,0) at the strike x=1, the forward, backward and central quotients are 1, 0 and 0.5 for every Δx. The central value looks like a delta but is not a derivative; numerical Greeks near strikes and barriers need care (LM40).

導讀數值微分：步長不是越小越好

用差分估計導數（實務上叫 bump and reprice）有兩種誤差在拉鋸：截斷誤差隨步長 Δx 變小而變小（前向差分 O(Δx)、中央差分 O(Δx2)），捨入誤差卻隨 Δx 變小而變大（約 εm​/Δx，雙精度 εm​=2.22×10−16）。所以最佳步長在中間：前向差分約 10−8、中央差分約 10−6（乘上問題的尺度）。實務上算債券 duration 用 1 bp 的中央差分就很準：誤差只有 1.8×10−6（相對誤差約 2×10−7）；但碰到買權履約價這種尖角，任何步長都算不出真正的導數。

Knowledge Check 7

Where truncation error dominates, by what factor does halving the step divide the forward error, and the central error? Check with h(x)=lnx at x=2, using Δx=0.01 and Δx=0.005.

Answer

By about 2 and about 4. For lnx at 2 the forward errors are −0.0012458 and −0.0006240 (ratio 2.00); the central errors are +4.167×10−6 and +1.042×10−6 (ratio 4.00).

9Derivatives in Python

implement and verify derivatives in Python with finite differences and symbolic differentiation

Three habits make derivatives safe in code. Compare every numerical derivative with an exact one on a case where both exist. Bump with central differences and a step well above the rounding floor. And let a computer algebra system check hand-derived formulas.

The first block implements (2.11) and reproduces Example 10:

Python
def bond_price(y, coupon=0.02, n=10, face=100.0):
    """Annual-coupon bond priced at yield y; the 10-year 2% bond by default."""
    return (sum(coupon * face / (1 + y) ** t for t in range(1, n + 1))
            + face / (1 + y) ** n)

def forward_diff(fun, x, dx):
    return (fun(x + dx) - fun(x)) / dx

def central_diff(fun, x, dx):
    return (fun(x + dx) - fun(x - dx)) / (2 * dx)

y0, dy = 0.02, 1e-4
P0 = bond_price(y0)
print(f"D_mod forward {-forward_diff(bond_price, y0, dy) / P0:.6f}")  # 8.977887
print(f"D_mod central {-central_diff(bond_price, y0, dy) / P0:.6f}")  # 8.982587

SymPy differentiates the same function symbolically and checks the leverage derivative of Example 4:

Python
import sympy as sp

y = sp.symbols("y", positive=True)
P = (sum(sp.Integer(2) / (1 + y) ** t for t in range(1, 11))
     + 100 / (1 + y) ** 10)
dP = sp.diff(P, y)                                     # exact derivative
print(sp.N(dP.subs(y, sp.Rational(1, 50)), 10))        # -898.2585006
print(sp.N((-dP / P).subs(y, sp.Rational(1, 50)), 6))  # 8.98259

F, E0, F0, N, m = sp.symbols("F E_0 F_0 N m", positive=True)
f = N * m * F / (E0 + N * m * (F - F0))                # exposure / equity
print(sp.simplify(sp.diff(f, F) + f * (f - 1) / F))    # 0, so f'(F) = -f(f-1)/F

Elasticities can be estimated from data. The account of the motivating case takes a few lines of Polars, and the slope of Example 8 one call to NumPy:

Python
import numpy as np
import polars as pl

# paths from the repository root
tx = pl.read_csv("data/raw/TX__2025-04-01__2025-10-31.csv")
june = (tx.filter(pl.col("contract_date") == 202506)
          .filter(pl.col("date").is_in(["2025-06-10", "2025-06-11"]))
          .sort("date")["settlement_price"].to_numpy())
f_A = 200 * june[0] / 600_000  # exposure / equity
print(f"f_A = {f_A:.4f}, account return = "
      f"{f_A * (june[1] / june[0] - 1):.2%}")  # 7.3720, 7.60%

# written by data/build_series.py
etf = pl.read_parquet("data/processed/etf_daily_returns.parquet")
slope = np.polyfit(etf["R_0050"].to_numpy(), etf["R_00631L"].to_numpy(), 1)[0]
print(f"elasticity of 00631L to 0050: {slope:.3f}")  # 1.887
In PythonCompanion lab

The notebook LM02_lab.ipynb rebuilds Exhibit 1, Exhibit 2, Exhibit 3, Exhibit 7, Exhibit 8, Exhibit 9 and Exhibit 10. It runs finite-difference experiments on a log–log grid and computes duration by bumping yields. It also estimates the elasticity of levered positions from 0050 data and solves the computational practice problems. The notebook reads FinMind files that you download once with your own token. From the repository root, run uv run python data/fetch_finmind.py, then uv run python data/make_lab_data.py. FinMind's licence does not allow the book to redistribute the data. After that, the notebook runs offline.

Summary

  • A limit describes where a function is heading. From 1+x≤ex≤1/(1−x) and the squeeze theorem, (ex−1)/x→1 and ln(1+x)/x→1; these two limits drive every derivative of exponentials and logarithms.
  • A function is continuous when its limit equals its value; discontinuities are removable, jumps (digital payoffs) or infinite (leverage at zero equity). A call payoff is continuous but not differentiable at the strike.
  • The derivative (2.4) is a rate with units: a slope, a marginal rate and a sensitivity. Six rules proved from (2.4) differentiate every function built from powers, exponentials and logarithms.
  • A futures position's delta is Nm NT$ per point (TX 200, MTX 50, TMF 10). Modified duration is −P′(y)/P, and Macaulay duration emerges as the present-value-weighted time; the 10-year 2% par bond has Dmod​=8.9826.
  • Elasticity is dlnh/dlnx. A futures account's equity elasticity equals its leverage f=NmF/E, exposure ÷ equity, exactly for one mark-to-market period. On 11 June 2025, f=7.3720 turned a 1.031% futures move into a 7.60% account move.
  • The leverage of a fixed position has elasticity 1−f. Account A's leverage fell from 7.37 to 2.89 in the June–October 2025 rally; account B's rose from 4.73 to 44.29 in three April sessions.
  • A linear approximation has error O((x−x0​)2) and fails for large moves, near singularities, at kinks and jumps, and at stationary points.
  • Numerical derivatives trade truncation error (O(Δx) forward, O(Δx2) central) against rounding error (of order εm​/Δx). Best steps are near 10−8 and 10−6 times the problem's scale; a 1 bp central bump prices duration to within 0.000002.

Practice Problems

  1. limx→0​(e2x−1)/x is:

    • A.1
    • B.2
    • C.e2

  2. The derivative of h(x)=ln(1+3x) at x=0 is:

    • A.1/3
    • B.1
    • C.3

  3. Use the definition (2.4) to find the derivative of h(x)=x​ at x=4.

  4. Which statement is correct?

    • A.Every differentiable function is continuous.
    • B.Every continuous function is differentiable.
    • C.The payoff max(S−K,0) is differentiable at S=K.

  5. A trader is long 1 TX, short 3 MTX and long 7 TMF in the same expiry month. Compute the position's delta and its profit if the futures price falls 250 points.

  6. An account holds 2 MTX contracts at F=25,000 with NT$500,000 of equity. If the futures price rises 1.2%, the account's return is closest to:

    • A.2.4%
    • B.5.0%
    • C.6.0%

  7. A futures account has leverage f=8. Using (2.9), estimate its leverage after the futures price rises 2% and after it falls 2%. Compute both exactly and explain why the linear estimate is worse for the fall.

  8. A 5-year zero-coupon bond yields 2%. Compute its modified duration under annual compounding and its duration under continuous compounding.

  9. A bond pays an annual coupon C per 100 face for n years and trades at par at its yield y0​, so C=100y0​. Show that its modified duration is Dmod​=(1−(1+y0​)−n)/y0​, the annuity factor an,i​ at i=y0​. Check the formula for the 10-year 2% bond.

  10. A Taiwan investor's USD fund returns RUSD=+8% over a year, while the exchange rate, TWD per USD, returns RFX=−5%. Compute the TWD return exactly and to first order, and identify the neglected term.

  11. Estimate the derivative of lnx at x=2 with forward and central differences using Δx=0.01. Report each error.

  12. In double precision, the step that minimizes the total error of a central difference for a function and argument of order 1 is closest to:

    • A.10−16
    • B.10−6
    • C.10−8

  13. A bet returns +2% or −1% with equal probability, and a trader stakes the fraction f of capital on it. The expected log growth per bet is g(f)=21​ln(1+0.02f)+21​ln(1−0.01f). Compute g′(f), evaluate it at f=0, 10, 25 and 40, and interpret the signs.

  14. The current yield of a bond with annual coupon C is CY(y)=C/P(y). Show that CY′(y)=CY⋅Dmod​, and estimate the change in the 10-year 2% bond's current yield for a 10 bp rise in its yield.

  15. Index futures fair value is F=Se(rf​−q)τ. Take S=22,470.10, rf​=1.6%, q=3.0% and τ=0.25 (illustrative inputs). Compute F, the elasticity of F with respect to S, and the change in F when q rises by 0.1 percentage point.

  16. (Python) Compute forward and central estimates of the 10-year bond's P′(2%) for Δy=10−1,10−2,…,10−12. Which step is best for each method, and how do the answers compare with Δy∗≈εm​​ and εm1/3​?

Solutions

  1. B is correct. With z=2x, (e2x−1)/x=2(ez−1)/z→2 by (2.2). A ignores the factor 2; C confuses the limit with e2x at x=1.

  2. C is correct. By the chain rule, h′(x)=3/(1+3x), so h′(0)=3. A inverts the inner derivative; B forgets it.

  3. Δx4+Δx​−2​=Δx(4+Δx​+2)(4+Δx)−4​=4+Δx​+21​→41​. So the derivative is 0.25, in agreement with 21​x−1/2 at x=4.

  4. A is correct (Section 3). B fails for ∣x∣ at 0. C fails because the left and right derivatives at K are 0 and 1.

  5. Delta is 200−3×50+7×10=120 NT$ per point. A 250-point fall loses 120×250= NT$30,000.

  6. C is correct. Notional is 2×50×25,000= NT$2,500,000, so f=2,500,000/500,000=5.0, and the return is 5.0×1.2%=6.0% exactly. A is twice the move (the number of contracts); B is the leverage itself.

  7. By (2.9) the elasticity is 1−8=−7. Linear estimates: 8×(1−7×0.02)=6.88 after the rise and 8×(1+7×0.02)=9.12 after the fall. Exactly, f=8×1.02/(1+8×0.02)=7.0345 after the rise and 8×0.98/(1−8×0.02)=9.3333 after the fall. The fall moves the account toward zero equity, where f curves sharply upward (Section 7), so the tangent line falls further behind.

  8. Annual compounding: Dmod​=5/1.02=4.9020. Continuous compounding: dPV/dr=−5PV, so the duration is exactly 5.0000. The two differ by the factor 1+y: modified duration is Macaulay duration (here 5) divided by 1+y, and continuous compounding removes that factor.

  9. Let v=1/(1+y) and an,y​=(1−vn)/y, so that P(y)=Can,y​+100vn. The chain rule gives dyd​vn=−nvn+1, and the quotient rule gives dyd​an,y​=[nyvn+1−(1−vn)]/y2. At y=y0​, where C=100y0​:

    P′(y0​)=100[y0​ny0​vn+1−(1−vn)​−nvn+1]=−100y0​1−vn​=−100an,y0​​.
    Since P(y0​)=100 at par, Dmod​=−P′/P=an,y0​​. For y0​=2% and n=10, an,y0​​=8.9826, matching Example 6.

  10. Exactly, 1.08×0.95−1=+2.6000%. To first order, 8%−5%=+3.00%. The neglected term is the cross product RUSDRFX=0.08×(−0.05)=−0.4000%, which is second order; log returns add without it.

  11. Forward: (ln2.01−ln2)/0.01=0.4987542, error −0.0012458. Central: (ln2.01−ln1.99)/0.02=0.500004167, error +4.167×10−6. The exact value is 0.5; the central estimate is about 300 times more accurate.

  12. B is correct. The best central step scales like εm1/3​=6.1×10−6. C is the best forward step, εm​​; A is machine epsilon itself, where rounding destroys the quotient.

  13. g′(f)=1+0.02f0.01​−1−0.01f0.005​. Then g′(0)=0.00500, the arithmetic mean return; g′(10)=0.002778; g′(25)=0; g′(40)=−0.002778. Growth rises with f up to f=25 and falls beyond it, so f∗=25 maximizes growth. LM4 develops this first-order condition and explains why such a large f should not be used as is.

  14. By the quotient rule, CY′=−CP′/P2=(C/P)⋅(−P′/P)=CY⋅Dmod​. For the 10-year bond, CY=2.0000% and CY′=0.02×8.9826=0.17965, so a 10 bp rise lifts the current yield by about 0.17965×0.001=1.80 bp. Exact repricing, 2/P(2.1%)=2/99.1064, gives 2.01803%, also +1.80 bp.

  15. F=22,470.10e(0.016−0.030)×0.25=22,391.6. Since F is proportional to S, ηF,S​=1 exactly, although dF/dS=e(rf​−q)τ=0.996506. dF/dq=−τF=−5,597.9 per unit of q, so a rise of 0.001 in q lowers F by 5.60 points.

  16. The scan reproduces Exhibit 10. The central error is smallest at Δy=10−6 (relative error 6.9×10−11). On this grid the forward error is smallest at 10−10 (4.2×10−8), but 10−9 (5.3×10−8) and 10−8 (6.1×10−8) are within a factor of 1.5 of it: a plateau around the crossover of the two error terms at 3×10−9.

    At 10−8 truncation still dominates (5.2×10−8 against 4.9×10−9 of rounding in the model). Below the crossover rounding dominates, and the low value at 10−10 (model 4.9×10−7) is luck. The quarter-decade scan of Exhibit 9 puts the minima at 10−8.25 and 10−5.75, which match εm​​=1.5×10−8 and εm1/3​=6.1×10−6 in order of magnitude.

Glossary

Term 中文 Meaning
Limit 極限 Value ℓ approached by h(x) as x→x0​, regardless of h(x0​).
One-sided limit 單邊極限 Limit as x approaches x0​ from the left or from the right only.
Squeeze theorem 夾擠定理 A function trapped between two functions with a common limit shares that limit.
Continuity 連續性 limx→x0​​h(x)=h(x0​).
Difference quotient 差商 [h(x0​+Δx)−h(x0​)]/Δx, the slope of a secant line.
Derivative 導數 Limit of the difference quotient, (2.4); a rate with units.
Tangent line 切線 Line through (x0​,h(x0​)) with slope h′(x0​).
Mean value theorem 均值定理 Some interior point has instantaneous rate equal to the average rate.
Chain rule 連鎖律 dxd​h(u(x))=h′(u(x))u′(x), (2.5).
Sensitivity 敏感度 Change in value per unit change in one risk factor, others fixed.
Contract multiplier 契約乘數 NT$ value of one index point for one futures contract.
Notional value 名目價值（契約價值） Multiplier × futures price × number of contracts: the exposure.
Delta Delta Derivative of a position's value with respect to the underlying price.
Modified duration 修正存續期間 −P′(y)/P, (2.6).
Macaulay duration 麥考利存續期間 Present-value-weighted average time of cash flows; (1+y)Dmod​.
DV01 基點價值 Price fall for a one-basis-point rise in yield, −P′(y)×0.0001.
Elasticity 彈性 dlnh/dlnx, the percentage change in h per 1% change in x, (2.7).
Leverage 槓桿倍數 Exposure ÷ equity, f=NmF/E; the equity elasticity of a futures account, (2.8).
Initial margin 原始保證金 Equity required per contract to open a futures position.
Maintenance margin 維持保證金 Equity level below which a margin call is triggered.
Differential 微分 dh=h′(x0​)dx, the change along the tangent line.
Linear approximation 線性近似 T1​(x)=h(x0​)+h′(x0​)(x−x0​); error O((x−x0​)2), (2.10).
Forward difference 前向差分 [h(x+Δx)−h(x)]/Δx; truncation error O(Δx).
Central difference 中央差分 [h(x+Δx)−h(x−Δx)]/(2Δx); truncation error O(Δx2).
Truncation error 截斷誤差 Error from replacing a limit by a finite step.
Rounding error 捨入誤差 Error from finite-precision arithmetic.
Machine epsilon 機器精度 Gap between 1 and the next double-precision number, 2.22×10−16.
